9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: 25 and 73

The piece is built on a six-motif rotation mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening. In every regular six-line stanza the six motifs occur once each, and the last motif of a stanza is the first motif of the next stanza.

1-6 : mountains valleys forests music morning evening
7-12: evening mountains morning valleys music forests
13-18: forests evening music mountains valleys morning
19-24: morning forests music valleys evening mountains
etc.

Following the chain the fifth Strephon stanza, lines 25-30, should open with music, because 24 ends with music, and it should then run music morning mountains forests evening valleys. 

The stanza as printed opens with

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

which contains two motifs at once, forests and music, and then repeats forests again at line 28. The stanza is therefore broken and the chain is interrupted.

The closing three lines are meant to be the paired-motif coda that closes the debate:

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

Lines 73 and 75 are the conventional two-motif coda lines, mountains+valleys and morning+evening. A single-motif music line is needed to open the fifth stanza and to keep the 25-30 rotation intact, and a two-motif forests+music line is needed to complete the paired coda.

Line 73 is the two-motif line that belongs in the coda position and line 25 is the two-motif line that is intruding into the regular six-line stanza. Restoring the rotation is achieved by exchanging the intruding line 25 with the coda line 73. With that exchange the fifth stanza becomes

Long since… my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;
Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
Long since I see my joys come to their evening,
And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys;

music morning mountains forests evening valleys, and the final triad is restored to the intended paired-motif form.

public_text.9:
25 and 73

The piece is built on a six-motif rotation mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening. In every regular six-line stanza the six motifs occur once each, and the last motif of a stanza is the first motif of the next stanza.

1-6 : mountains valleys forests music morning evening
7-12: evening mountains morning valleys music forests
13-18: forests evening music mountains valleys morning
19-24: morning forests music valleys evening mountains
etc.

Following the chain the fifth Strephon stanza, lines 25-30, should open with music, because 24 ends with music, and it should then run music morning mountains forests evening valleys. 

The stanza as printed opens with

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

which contains two motifs at once, forests and music, and then repeats forests again at line 28. The stanza is therefore broken and the chain is interrupted.

The closing three lines are meant to be the paired-motif coda that closes the debate:

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

Lines 73 and 75 are the conventional two-motif coda lines, mountains+valleys and morning+evening. A single-motif music line is needed to open the fifth stanza and to keep the 25-30 rotation intact, and a two-motif forests+music line is needed to complete the paired coda.

Line 73 is the two-motif line that belongs in the coda position and line 25 is the two-motif line that is intruding into the regular six-line stanza. Restoring the rotation is achieved by exchanging the intruding line 25 with the coda line 73. With that exchange the fifth stanza becomes

Long since… my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;
Long since my thoughts more desert be than forests;
Long since I see my joys come to their evening,
And state thrown down to over-trodden valleys;

music morning mountains forests evening valleys, and the final triad is restored to the intended paired-motif form.

The poem is built as an extended sestina on the six end-words mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening. The six-line stanzas keep the classic retrogradation 6 1 5 2 4 3 and the speakers cycle A-B-C for Strephon and D-E-F for Klaius, so the end-word pattern is intact through stanza 12.

The three-line envoi has to close the sestina by containing the six end-words. In the text as printed we have

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

That is mountains + valleys, music, morning + evening. Forests is absent from the envoi, while the stanza material contains an anomalous double-motif line

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

which is the only stanza line that carries two of the sestina terms inside it, forests at the head and music at the tail, and it also breaks the normal subject-verb agreement with the next line Hath made itself a crier of the morning. The singular subject my deadly swannish music in the envoi is the natural antecedent for Hath made itself.

Moving the forests-bearing material into the envoi and restoring a single-motif stanza line restores the envoi to mountains/valleys, forests/music, morning/evening and gives line 25 a normal single-motif music ending. The first envoi position is the one that has been displaced, i.e. 73 with 25.

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

26 and 74

The six-line Strephon stanzas are built as a single grammatical chain. In the present text Strephon’s 25-30 block opens:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
26 Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
27 And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

Line 26 opens with the finite verb “Hath made itself…” with no grammatical antecedent in the immediately preceding line. The subject that belongs with that verb-chain is the subject-phrase that now sits at the close of the dialogue:

74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

Placed before the Hath-verb the chain reads naturally:

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music / Hath made itself a crier of the morning, / And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

The same displacement is visible at the close. Strephon’s final witness line

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;

is left hanging before the orphaned subject-phrase in 74, and the witness couplet is restored when the forest line that now sits in 25 is moved to the Klaius position, giving a coherent closing witness to mountains, valleys and forests before the shared

75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

Once 26 and 74 are exchanged the subject-verb dependency in the 25-27 chain is restored and the antiphonal closing is parallel again.

Line 73 is correct: mountains in the middle, valleys at the end. Line 75 is correct: morning in the middle, evening at the end. Line 74 is the problem: it ends with music, as the second tornada line must, but it supplies no interior forests to pair with it.

The only line in the whole poem that ends in music and carries forests in its interior is line 25,

These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

so that is the line that belongs in the tornada. The line that is sitting in the tornada now, Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music, is a perfectly good music-ending lament, and it is the one that is sitting in the fifth sestina position where a music-ending line is expected. The closest thematic and metrical match for it inside the body of the poem is

For she whose parts maintained a perfect music,

line 61, which also ends in music and which sits in the 4-5-1-3-6-2 stanza as the opening music-ending line. Putting line 61 into the tornada and bringing the forests + music line 25 back into the body restores the tornada’s required forests-music pairing and restores the normal lament tone of the fifth stanza. The transposition is the one that breaks the otherwise perfect end-word rotation.

The six revolving termini are mountains 1, valleys 2, forests 3, music 4, morning 5, evening 6. Lines 1-72 are the ordinary double sestina

1 2 3 4 5 6
6 1 5 2 4 3
3 6 4 1 2 5
5 3 2 6 1 4
4 5 1 3 6 2
2 4 6 5 3 1

repeated for the second cycle, and the end-word chain is intact through 72.

The envoi is supposed to be the 1-2 / 3-4 / 5-6 couplet. As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1-2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music             4
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.          5-6

73 is correct 1-2, 75 is correct 5-6, and the 3-4 forests-music couplet is missing from the tornada. The only line in the whole body which both contains forests in the interior and ends in music is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

That is the line that belongs in the middle of the envoi. The problem is the partner of the transposition.

The standard 25 ↔ 74 account keeps the end-word of stanza 5 unchanged because both lines end in music, and that is why the error is hard to see on a purely lexical check. That is also why it is editorially implausible. 25 is Strephon and 74 is Klaius. A compositor’s transposition in this dialogue sestina would almost certainly stay inside a speaker block; crossing the Strephon/Klaius boundary and moving a Klaius tornada line into a Strephon sestet is a very different kind of accident from a simple mis-ordered leaf within Strephon’s own speech.

The Strephon material that is actually sitting in the closing position is

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;

that is the Strephon line that has been displaced into the envoi. 25 is the intruding forests/music line that has been displaced down into Strephon’s fifth sestet. Putting the forests/music material back into the envoi and restoring a proper Strephon envoi line to the body restores the six-word inventory of the tornada to

73 ← 25   These forests eke, made wretched by our music;   3-4
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.          5-6

with 73 now supplying the 1-2 mountains/valleys material in the body where a mountains/valleys ending is required in the Strephon block that carries the witness couplet. The envoi is then mountains/valleys, forests/music, morning/evening as the sestina demands, and the speaker alternation Strephon – Klaius – Both is preserved in the closing three lines.

The intruding line is 25 and the line it has been transposed with is the first tornada line, 73.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The twelve six-line blocks are a double sestina on mountains / valleys / forests / music / morning / evening and the retrogradatio is intact through line 72. The only thing that is broken is the three-line envoi.

In the print we have

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; 1-2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music          4
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.     5-6

73 is 1 in the middle / 2 at the close and 75 is 5 in the middle / 6 at the close. The middle envoi line is therefore required to be 3 + 4, forests in the middle and music at the close. The body contains exactly one line which does that work in a single line:

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

25 is the intruder in Strephon’s fifth sestet. It ends in music, so moving it out of the stanza does not disturb the 4-5-1-3-6-2 end-word set of lines 25-30, and it is the only line in the whole piece that can supply the missing forests + music couplet to the envoi.

What has to come back into the body in its place is the music-ending line that belongs to the “Long since … Hath made itself … And hath…” chain that opens Strephon’s fifth sestet. The printed line 26

Hath made itself a crier of the morning,

is verbally orphaned. The natural subject for Hath made itself / And hath with wailing strength… is the subject phrase that is now sitting in the envoi,

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

which is a continuation of the Long since… motif that runs through 28-29, 31, 33-35. Put that subject back at the head of the chain and the stanza reads

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music
Hath made itself a crier of the morning,
And hath with wailing strength climbed highest mountains;

music morning mountains and the sestina rotation is restored. The line that is displaced from the envoi into the body is therefore the first envoi line as printed, 73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys; and the forests/music line that belongs in the envoi is 25. Restoring

73 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;
74 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.

gives the envoi the required 3-4 / 1-2 / 5-6 disposition and gives Strephon’s fifth sestet a grammatical subject for its Hath-chain. The two transposed texts are 25 and 73.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The double sestina analysis is right. The six end-words are mountains 1, valleys 2, forests 3, music 4, morning 5, evening 6 and the 12 × 6 body is the regular retrogradatio cruciata through line 72. The coda has to be the 1-2 / 3-4 / 5-6 envoi.

As printed

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;   1-2
74 Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music                4
75 Our morning hymn is this, and song at evening.           5-6

73 is mountains/valleys and 75 is morning/evening, 3-forests is missing from the envoi. The only line in the whole body which contains both 3 forests in the middle and 4 music at the close is

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

which is the line that belongs in the middle envoi position. Line 25 is the body intruder.

The partner cannot be the Klaius tornada line 74. 74 is

Long since, alas, my deadly swannish music

and the “Long since” anaphora is a Klaius signature. Lines 31-36 and 55-60 are all Klaius “Long since” sequences, and 74 continues that Klaius diction. Moving a Klaius “Long since” line into Strephon’s 25-30 sestet would break the speaker alternation and the anaphoric fabric of the dialogue. The displacement has to stay inside Strephon.

The Strephon line that is sitting in the envoi place is 73. 73 is a Strephon witness line and it is the line that has been put into the tornada in place of the forests/music couplet. Put

25 These forests eke, made wretched by our music;

into the envoi and put

73 These mountains witness shall, so shall these valleys;

back into the body where its Strephon voice belongs. The envoi then becomes

73 mountains/valleys
74 forests/music
75 morning/evening

i.e. 1-2 / 3-4 / 5-6, and the speaker integrity of the Strephon/Klaius alternation is preserved. The two transposed texts are therefore Strephon line 25 and the Strephon envoi line 73.
